title: Virtual Skin Manifold: Proprioceptive Contact Sensing for Humanoid Robots
description: Research at Figueroa GRASP Lab on a virtual skin manifold for full-body contact detection using only internal joint torque sensing — achieving 0.2 mm precision at 100 Hz via particle filtering, eliminating the need for external tactile skins (~$30,000 in hardware).
abstract: This research replaces external tactile skins with a proprioception-only contact sensing pipeline. We engineer a virtual skin manifold over the robot's morphology and run a high-frequency particle filter at 100 Hz over internal joint torque sensor streams to localize contact events with 0.2 mm spatial precision on humanoid hardware. Building on manufacturer-agnostic C++/Python data acquisition libraries for robot actuators (Franka arms, Castor Bot), we model current/torque inference characteristics analogous to proprioception in the human neuromuscular system. Ongoing work extends this to a GPU-accelerated voxel-based 3D shape learning pipeline in PyTorch that infers grasping and manipulation strategies for unknown objects in a blind state — no vision, contact sensing only.
venue: University of Pennsylvania — Figueroa GRASP Lab

title: Reinforcement Learning for Self-Reconfiguring Modular Robots
description: Research at Mod Lab: a PPO reinforcement learning policy for quadruped locomotion that generalizes across dynamically mutating morphologies, plus string actuators and multi-agent cognitive perception for the modular robotic platform Abott.
abstract: We architect a Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) reinforcement learning policy to drive autonomous locomotion adaptation for a quadruped robot, generalizing across dynamically mutating morphologies and terrain conditions. Training runs on GPU-accelerated simulation infrastructure built in Isaac Lab and MuJoCo with domain-randomized tensor workloads for rapid policy iteration. In parallel, we design and build string actuators for the Abott modular robotic platform and define a multi-agent system that analyzes proprioceptive actuator data for task cognitive perception — independent agents either reinforce motor control or mutate the physical agent configuration based on sensory inputs, enabling adaptive, self-reconfiguring robotic behavior.

title: Automated Quantum Control: Rabi Chevron Mapping on Liquid-State NMR
description: Research at the Quantum Hardware Lab: an automated quantum control software pipeline for a room-temperature liquid-state NMR system, sweeping RF pulses to map Rabi chevrons on nuclear spins — accelerating qubit calibration by 80%. Plus experimental validation of quantum algorithms on IBM Quantum hardware.
abstract: We engineered an automated quantum control software pipeline for a room-temperature liquid-state NMR system, programmatically sweeping radio-frequency (RF) pulses to map Rabi chevrons on the nuclear spins of a water molecule. By extracting optimal π-pulse durations and zero-detuning frequencies from the chevron interference patterns, physical qubit calibration time was accelerated by 80% — bridging high-level algorithmic intent with low-level hardware execution. The control apparatus uses the Digital Programmable Function Generator Moku-go for arbitrary function generation and quantum spin control of Hydrogen protons. Additionally, we developed interactive Python notebooks for ESE 5090 enabling hands-on experimental validation of quantum gates on real IBM devices via IBM Cloud, implementing Grover's, Shor's, Quantum Fourier Transform, Bernstein-Vazirani, Simon's Algorithm, and quantum cryptography protocols, with analysis of noise, decoherence, and gate fidelity against ideal simulation.
venue: University of Pennsylvania — Quantum Hardware Lab / ESE 5090 QHEL Lab

title: Sampling-Based and Convex MPC for F1Tenth Autonomous Racing
description: Formulated and implemented Model Predictive Control for the F1Tenth 1/10th-scale autonomous racing platform — a convex QP controller (CVXPY/OSQP) and a GPU-accelerated sampling-based MPPI controller evaluating 1000+ trajectory candidates per cycle at 50 Hz. Placed 2nd in the University Competition.
abstract: This work presents two MPC formulations for autonomous racing on a kinematic bicycle model with state space [x, y, θ, v]. First, a convex Quadratic Program (QP) minimizing trajectory deviation, input effort, and input rate of change subject to vehicle dynamic constraints — linearized via first-order Taylor expansion, discretized with Forward Euler, and solved each timestep using CVXPY with the OSQP backend. Second, a sampling-based MPPI controller implemented with JAX JIT compilation and vmap vectorization across 1000+ trajectory candidates per cycle, leveraging XLA for GPU kernel fusion to eliminate redundant memory transfers and achieve 50 Hz real-time inference on an NVIDIA Jetson. Both controllers were validated in F1Tenth simulation and on a physical car at UPenn, achieving 2nd place in the University Competition.
venue: University of Pennsylvania — ESE 615 / X-Lab (F1Tenth Autonomous Racing)

title: Computer Vision Pipeline for F1Tenth with Intel RealSense D435i
description: Designed a complete computer vision pipeline for an autonomous F1Tenth racing car using an Intel RealSense D435i camera mounted on a Jetson NX. The pipeline covers camera calibration, ground-plane distance measurement, lane detection, and object detection.
abstract: We built an integrated perception stack for an F1Tenth vehicle. Camera intrinsics were obtained via chessboard calibration (findChessboardCorners, calibrateCamera). Ground-plane distance estimation uses the calibrated intrinsic matrix and measured camera mounting height. Lane detection applies HSV color segmentation and contour-finding. A custom YOLO-like network was trained in PyTorch on a labeled F110 car dataset, converted to ONNX, and deployed via TensorRT 8.5 on the Jetson NX in both FP32 and FP16 modes. The full pipeline integrates all components to output detected lane boundaries and vehicle distances in real time at 60Hz.
venue: University of Pennsylvania — ESE 615 (F1Tenth Autonomous Racing)
